questions.q: How does AWS Organizations structure multiple accounts, compared to Azure's management group hierarchy?
options: AWS has no equivalent concept — every account is fully independent with no policy inheritance

Accounts are grouped under Organizational Units (OUs) in a tree rooted at the organization's root, with policies attached at an OU level inherited by accounts beneath it — structurally the same idea as management groups and subscriptions
AWS accounts automatically inherit policy from any other account in the same AWS region
OUs can only ever contain exactly one account each
questions.explain: AWS Organizations groups accounts under OUs the same structural way Azure groups subscriptions under management groups — a root, nested containers, and inherited policy.

questions.q: Which three accounts does AWS Control Tower create the first time it is enabled?
options: Management, Log Archive, and Audit accounts
Production, Staging, and Development accounts
Billing, Marketing, and Engineering accounts
Sandbox, Workloads, and Suspended accounts
questions.explain: Control Tower's initial setup creates a Management account (billing/administration), a dedicated Log Archive account for CloudTrail/Config data, and a dedicated Audit account for security tooling.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a preventive guardrail (a Service Control Policy) and a detective guardrail (an AWS Config rule)?
options: A detective guardrail blocks an API call outright, while a preventive guardrail only reports on it afterward
They are two names for the exact same mechanism with no functional difference

A preventive guardrail (SCP) blocks an API call outright regardless of IAM permissions, while a detective guardrail (Config rule) continuously evaluates existing resources and flags, but doesn't block, drift after the fact
Detective guardrails only apply to the Management account
questions.explain: SCPs sit above IAM and deny actions outright; Config rules evaluate resources that already exist and flag non-compliance without blocking it.

questions.q: Why can't an IAM policy inside an account override a Service Control Policy denying that same action at the OU level?
options: SCPs sit above IAM in the evaluation — they are a separate, higher layer that can deny an action regardless of what any IAM policy in the account grants
IAM policies always take priority over SCPs by default
SCPs only apply to the root account and never to member accounts
SCPs and IAM policies are evaluated independently and whichever is more permissive wins
questions.explain: The guide is explicit: an SCP denying an action means no IAM policy inside any account in that OU can override it — SCPs sit above IAM, not alongside it.

questions.q: What is Account Factory for Terraform (AFT), and how does it relate to subscription vending from Lesson 6?
options: A tool that deletes AWS accounts automatically after 90 days of inactivity
AFT replaces Control Tower entirely and no longer uses Organizations or SCPs
AFT only works for Azure subscriptions, not AWS accounts

The Terraform-driven equivalent of Control Tower's Account Factory, taking account requests as Terraform configuration — the direct AWS counterpart to the Terraform-based subscription vending module covered for Azure
questions.explain: AFT lets teams provision new, already-compliant AWS accounts through Terraform instead of Control Tower's console workflow, mirroring the subscription vending module pattern from Lesson 6 on the same Course 8 skill set.
